label: context.reference
text:
Octopus is organized through interfaces, artifacts, runs and goal-classified Execution Environments (EEs). Models and clients are interfaces; the runtime forms policy, routes artifacts and records evidence. Interface packages interpret their own inputs and outputs.

An interface's registry folder is its routing identity. Active checkpoints bind those identities; artifact names and any declared verified requirements determine which arrivals they admit. A route without requirements remains available for later distinct artifacts. A verified wait is spent when its requirement set closes. Runs are durable records, including their waits, rather than processes that must keep running.

Authority is the worker pin's ceiling intersected with its EE chain and authored bindings. Worker environments provide tools and permitted paths for effects. Descriptions and copied configurations grant no authority. Roles, skills, knowledge and context are readable artifacts reached through bindings.

To change behavior, locate the interface or room that owns it and follow the relevant artifact from its producer to its consumer. Inspect the current declarations and, when necessary, that owner's code. An existing family can often express the change through JSON. A new execution family belongs in an owner package. Keep the kernel independent of product, provider and task names.

Changes to records and descriptors use granted file tools; other effects use their declared interfaces. Protect concurrent edits and retain admitted effects and their evidence. File edits change the declarations used by later arrivals; the ledger records the movements that actually occurred. Investigate a refusal at the boundary that produced it.
description: Octopus primitives and authority; find the owner and trace the behavior being changed.
